text: An IP address gets traffic to the right host. A port number gets it to the right application on that host. Ports run 0 to 65,535, and the first 1,023 are well-known ports — reserved by convention for specific standard services. This lesson is the exact list a working analyst is expected to recognize on sight.

FTP uses ports 20 and 21 for file transfer. SSH on port 22 is encrypted remote login. Telnet on port 23 is its unencrypted, legacy predecessor — avoid it. SMTP on port 25 sends email between mail servers. DNS on port 53 resolves domain names to IP addresses. HTTP on port 80 is unencrypted web traffic.

POP3 on port 110 and IMAP on port 143 both retrieve email, but POP3 downloads and often deletes from the server while IMAP syncs across devices. HTTPS on port 443 is encrypted web traffic. SMB on port 445 handles Windows file and printer sharing. MySQL listens on 3306. RDP, Windows Remote Desktop, uses port 3389.

A SOC analyst reads the destination port in a log line before anything else, because it names the probable service instantly. Unexpected inbound traffic on port 3389, RDP, at two in the morning gets flagged immediately — it's one of the most common ransomware entry points on record. Telnet showing up on port 23 at all is often itself the finding, since it sends credentials in plaintext.

Ports are a convention, not an enforced rule. Attackers hide command-and-control traffic on port 443 to blend in with normal HTTPS, and WannaCry spread in 2017 by scanning for open port 445. That's why experienced analysts treat a port number as a strong hint worth investigating, never a guarantee of what's actually inside the traffic.

Memorizing this list is non-negotiable for Network+ and Security+, and for the job itself — there's no time to look each one up mid-incident. Next up: how the real protocols behind these ports — web, email, and file transfer — actually work.
